source: Katebi, Sakallah, Marques-Silva (2011) Empirical Study of the Anatomy of Modern SAT Solvers (SAT 2011)
finding: Ablation of a MiniSat-style solver, switching off one CDCL feature at a time. Clause learning matters most, then VSIDS, then two-watched-literals, then restarts.
numbers: 1000 instances from 12 application families x 10 seeded versions x 15 MiniSat configurations = 150,000 runs, 1000 s limit. Full CDCL solved 9068 of 10000 instance-versions. Without learning: 4837. Without VSIDS (DLIS): 6932. Without 2WL: 8409. Without restarts: 8653. Extra instances solved by enabling CL, VSIDS, 2WL, RST: 4231, 2136, 659, 415.
limits: One solver family (MiniSat). Instance-level counts, not time. Time-outs handled by maximum-likelihood estimates. Only 71% of averages are within 25% at 90% confidence.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G-level claim that remembering why an attempt failed is the biggest single lever in a search loop; restart-like resets are the smallest of the four.

source: Katebi, Sakallah, Marques-Silva (2011) Empirical Study of the Anatomy of Modern SAT Solvers (SAT 2011)
finding: Restarts help on average but not always. They help SAT instances more than UNSAT. On the termrw family, more instances were solved with restarts off.
numbers: Luby restarts on: 4533 SAT and 4535 UNSAT solved, 932 timeouts. Restarts off: 4230 SAT, 4423 UNSAT, 1347 timeouts. termrw family: 420 solved with restarts (250 SAT, 170 UNSAT) vs 446 without (252 SAT, 194 UNSAT).
quote: the effect of restarts is not always predictable
limits: Family-level exception, single solver. Cause not analysed.
agent_relevance: A reset-and-retry operator has a positive mean effect but a family-dependent sign. Keep it conditional and keep the no-goods across it.

source: Katebi, Sakallah, Marques-Silva (2011) Empirical Study of the Anatomy of Modern SAT Solvers (SAT 2011)
finding: Randomness and small variations in the branching rule are not harmless. Fully random branching beat the DLIS rule overall. Adding a little randomness to VSIDS helped one family by up to 13 instances.
numbers: Random branching (rnd-freq=100) solved 7325 vs DLIS 6932. Some option tweaks gave up to 13 more (VSIDS randomness) or 9 more (clause minimisation off) hverif instances.
limits: Authors say they cannot explain all of this without instance-level study.
agent_relevance: Diversity of choice order matters less than keeping the learned constraints; a cheap random tie-break is a defensible default.

source: Moskewicz, Madigan, Zhao, Zhang, Malik (2001) Chaff: Engineering an Efficient SAT Solver (DAC 2001)
finding: Chaff beat GRASP and SATO by one to two orders of magnitude on hard industrial instances. The authors say the gain came from engineering (fast propagation, a decision rule focused on recent conflict clauses), not from smarter learning.
numbers: SSS.1.0: about 10x faster, all done in 100 s. SSS-SAT.1.0: Chaff finished 100 of 100 in under 1000 s (100 s cap each); SATO aborted 32 of the first 41. VLIW-SAT.1.0: Chaff finished 100 in under 10000 s; GRASP and SATO aborted the first 19 of 20 tried. Run on a 336 MHz UltraSparc machine.
quote: This speedup is not the result of sophisticated learning strategies for pruning the search space
limits: Authors could not reproduce GRASP's published randomised-restart results (config unavailable). Comparison is cross-solver, so many factors are mixed. Old hardware and benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation to 'learning is the key': cheap bookkeeping plus a recency-weighted focus rule can matter as much. For an LLM agent: how cheaply failures are recorded and recalled is part of the effect.

source: Moskewicz et al. (2001) Chaff
finding: Chaff's restarts keep all learned clauses and may fire thousands of times per hard instance, yet similar results are often reachable with restarts disabled. Completeness is kept by slowly growing the restart period or the clause relevance parameter.
numbers: Restart count: 'thousands of times on a hard instance' (default settings).
quote: similar results can often (or at least sometimes) be achieved with restarts completely disabled
limits: Qualitative statement, no ablation table in this paper.
agent_relevance: Restarts only make sense when the no-good store survives them (this is the CDCL feature to copy).

source: Bayardo and Schrag (1997) Using CSP Look-Back Techniques to Solve Real-World SAT Instances (AAAI-97)
finding: Adding backjumping and relevance-bounded learning (relsat) made a plain Davis-Putnam solver match or beat the stochastic solvers WSAT and GSAT on many planning, scheduling and circuit instances. Relevance-bounded learning was the most useful addition. Simple size-bounded learning was weaker, and fourth-order size-bounded learning lost to third-order because of overhead.
numbers: Beijing planning: 3blocks solved 100% in 6.0 s (relsat(3)) and 6.4 s (relsat(4)); 4blocksb 100% in 79 and 55 s; 4blocks failure rate 34% (relsat(3)) and 17% (relsat(4)), mean 406 and 333 s near the cutoff. Naivesat solved neither bridge-fault nor single-stuck-at instance within 10 min in 100 runs. Adding backjumping alone solved the bridge-fault instance in 100 of 100 runs; single-stuck-at still had 23 failures.
quote: Look-back for DP is not a "magic bullet"
limits: 1997 hardware (110 MHz SGI). Instances picked for difficulty. Run times normalised across machines by hand. Random 3SAT phase-transition instances gain little from look-back.
agent_relevance: Two lessons: forget a no-good once it is no longer relevant to the current partial assignment (relevance-bounded), and expect gains only where short no-goods exist.

source: Bayardo and Schrag (1997) Using CSP Look-Back Techniques (AAAI-97)
finding: Boundary condition from the authors: look-back helps when real-world instances contain sub-problems with short, easily derived no-goods. Some instances stayed hard for look-back DP but were easy or trivial for WSAT.
numbers: The 3bit circuit instances were never solved by any of the authors' Davis-Putnam look-back variants but were trivial for WSAT.
quote: real-world instances often contain subproblems with short, easily derived nogoods
limits: Authors' own interpretation, not tested by intervention.
agent_relevance: No-good recording pays off only if failures can be shrunk to short, reusable reasons. Test the shrinkage rate before building the store.

source: Audemard and Simon (2009) Predicting Learnt Clauses Quality in Modern SAT Solvers (IJCAI-09)
finding: Literal Block Distance (LBD) is a cheap static score that predicts which learned clauses will be useful. Clauses with LBD 2 ('glue clauses') are used far more than their size suggests. Using LBD to delete clauses aggressively improves results.
numbers: On SAT-Race 06 benchmarks (1000 s cap): 40% of unit propagations on learnt clauses come from glue clauses, only 20% from size-2 clauses. Half of learnt clauses used in conflict analysis have LBD < 6, but need size < 13 for the same share. MiniSat variants solved 70, 74, 79, 82 instances (original, +aggressive deletion, +LBD, +both; mapping of rows read from a garbled table).
quote: deleting useful clauses can be dramatic in practice
limits: Row-to-label mapping of Table 3 is uncertain in the text extraction; the 70-to-82 range is solid. Correlation of LBD with later use, not a causal test.
agent_relevance: Which stored lessons to keep is itself learnable: rank a lesson by how many separate 'decision blocks' it ties together, not by length.

source: Audemard and Simon (2009) Predicting Learnt Clauses Quality (IJCAI-09)
finding: Glucose (MiniSat core + LBD deletion + Luby restarts + phase saving) outperformed the SAT'07 competition winners on 234 industrial instances. It scaled better with extra time.
numbers: Solved (10000 s, 1 GB, 234 SAT'07 industrial instances): Glucose 176, PicoSat 153, RSat 139, MiniSat 132, MiniSat+ 136, zChaff 2001 84, zChaff 2004 80 (SAT/UNSAT split in paper). Glucose fastest on 68 instances. Glucose solved 140 problems in 2500 s; others needed 4000-10000 s.
limits: Authors' own solver on a competition set they chose to compare on; lead is largest on UNSAT. Unique-solve counts (#U) are noisy.
agent_relevance: Aggressive forgetting plus a quality score beat keeping everything. Capping the lesson store is not a loss if the cap is smart.

source: Audemard and Simon (2009) Predicting Learnt Clauses Quality (IJCAI-09)
finding: Mechanism claim: decision levels decrease along a run on most industrial instances, and the 'look-back justification' tracks effort. Keeping learned clauses that shrink the number of decision levels is what helps.
numbers: Across 199 benchmarks, 92% show a decreasing decision level; median look-back justification 1.5x10^5 conflicts; fitted effective conflicts about 1.37x the justification.
limits: Regression on SAT-Race style structured instances only. Authors say the point is the strong relationship, not time prediction.
agent_relevance: Suggests a progress measure for the agent: are later attempts conflicting at shallower depth? If not, the stored no-goods are not working.

source: Elffers, Giraldez-Cru, Gocht, Nordstrom, Simon (2018) Seeking Practical CDCL Insights from Theoretical SAT Benchmarks (IJCAI-18)
finding: Using crafted formulas with short resolution proofs, they show learned clauses are absolutely critical, not just a source of guidance for branching. Too-aggressive clause erasure hurts when memory is tight, and LBD often picks the right clauses to keep.
numbers: Only unsatisfiable formulas; instrumented Glucose with many settings (restarts, VSIDS decay, phase saving, clause erasure), scored by PAR and timeouts per family.
quote: Learned clauses are absolutely critical for performance.
limits: Unsatisfiable crafted families only. Correlation, with the authors warning it is not causation. Settings cannot reach the range where theoretical hardness is guaranteed.
agent_relevance: Settles a rival explanation: storing the lessons themselves, not just using conflicts to steer, is the part that scales.

source: Elffers et al. (2018) Seeking Practical CDCL Insights (IJCAI-18)
finding: Restarts: frequent restarts are important for some formula families (stone, pebbling), supporting the view that restarts add real reasoning power. Glucose adaptive restarts usually beat Luby but sometimes block restarts completely and perform terribly. On clique formulas restarts must be off.
numbers: Qualitative with plots; adaptive restarts 'go badly wrong' on some families where Luby works much better; clique family is the one clear exception needing restarts off.
limits: Authors cannot explain the clique result. Whether restarts are needed in theory is still open.
agent_relevance: Rule: never let a stall detector suppress restarts forever; mix an adaptive trigger with a fixed fallback.

source: Elffers et al. (2018) Seeking Practical CDCL Insights (IJCAI-18)
finding: Failed to confirm that the newer learning-rate branching (LRB) beats VSIDS. No single best VSIDS decay factor exists; for partial ordering formulas a high decay makes them impossible and a lower decay makes them easy.
numbers: LRB vs VSIDS(0.99): timeout difference per family near 0 with a few outliers favouring LRB. Random variable choice 'consistently a terrible option'; random phase is not catastrophic.
quote: we cannot see any support for the hypothesis that the new learning-rate based heuristic would be better than VSIDS
limits: Crafted unsatisfiable families may not represent industrial instances where LRB was tuned.
agent_relevance: Recency weighting (how fast to forget which options were involved in failure) is a tuned parameter with no universal setting. Expose it, do not hard-code it.

source: Biere and Frohlich (2015) Evaluating CDCL Restart Schemes (Pragmatics of SAT 2015)
finding: Fixed restart interval sweep in Lingeling on SAT Competition 2014 (300 instances). More instances solved with longer intervals up to 256, but UNSAT solved peaks at interval 8. SAT and UNSAT want different intervals. A uniform interval can match Luby overall but not per bucket.
limits: One solver (Lingeling), one competition year, 23 buckets of about 13 instances. Seed effect ruled out by authors for most buckets.
agent_relevance: Restart cadence should depend on whether the task is likely solvable (find a witness: restart rarely) or must be refuted (restart often). A detector for that is worth more than a fixed schedule.

source: Biere and Frohlich (2015) Evaluating CDCL Restart Schemes
finding: Glucose-style dynamic restarts re-done with exponential moving averages gave the best result. Instances solved in the same benchmark set.
numbers: Lingeling with EMA version of Glucose restarts: 178 solved; best EMA variant ema-14: 181. Best static interval (r=256): 168. Best Luby (base 2): 168. Inner/outer scheme best 161. Out of 300 instances.
limits: Gains of 10-13 instances on 300; no confidence interval. Authors tuned only the slow-EMA parameter.
agent_relevance: A cheap running average of recent progress is a better restart trigger than a fixed count.

source: Beame, Kautz, Sabharwal (2004) Towards Understanding and Harnessing the Potential of Clause Learning (JAIR 22)
finding: Theory: clause learning (even without restarts, with a good learning scheme) can give exponentially shorter proofs than regular, Davis-Putnam and tree-like resolution. With unlimited restarts a variant is as strong as full resolution. But finding such proofs depends on branching order.
numbers: Theorems 1 and 2. Exponential empirical speed-up over zChaff on grid and randomised pebbling formulas when a branching sequence from the problem graph is supplied (tables report zChaff out-of-memory where guided runs finish).
limits: The restart result needs a slightly modified learner and unlimited restarts. Real solvers do not follow the idealised nondeterministic choice. Pipatsrisawat and Darwiche (2011) later gave the stronger p-simulation of resolution by actual CDCL (not opened here).
agent_relevance: The store of no-goods is strong in principle, but only if the order in which the agent tries things is good. Problem structure should drive the order.

source: Rintanen (2010) Heuristics for Planning with SAT (CP 2010)
finding: In SAT-based planning, a planning-specific variable choice (backward chaining from goals) beats VSIDS inside the same CDCL solver. CDCL planner then competes with LAMA, the 2008 competition winner.
numbers: 968 STRIPS instances from IPC 1998-2008, 300 s each. Solved: VSIDS 701, new heuristic 757, LAMA 775, Precosat 610, RSAT 653 (column mapping read from table layout). Heuristic costs 5-30% of SAT time.
limits: Column labels read from a flattened table. Only plan-finding; plan length is longer (82.5 vs 61.2 actions on instances solved by both variants). Author's own solver.
agent_relevance: Analogue in planning: generic conflict-driven learning is kept, but the choice heuristic is replaced by domain structure. Same split for an agent: general no-good memory plus task-specific ordering.

source: Shinn, Cassano, Berman, Gopinath, Narasimhan, Yao (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: An LLM agent that writes a short verbal reflection after each failed trial and keeps the last 3 reflections raised success on AlfWorld, HotPotQA and HumanEval. It is the closest published form of recording failures to avoid repeats. The reflection is free text, not a checked constraint.
numbers: ALFWorld (134 tasks, 12 consecutive trials): ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134; ReAct alone plateaued between trials 6 and 7. Headline: +22% AlfWorld, +20% HotPotQA, +11% HumanEval over strong baselines. HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%.
limits: HotPotQA used 100 questions. ALFWorld retry loop triggers on a hand-written heuristic (same action and response more than 3 cycles, or over 30 actions). Test-based signal in code tasks is an oracle-like check. Memory capped at 3 reflections.
agent_relevance: Positive evidence for failure memory, with a cap on how many lessons enter the prompt.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Reflexion's own ablations show where the gain comes from and where it fails. The written lesson matters (not only replaying the last trajectory). Reflection without tests hurts. On MBPP Python it did worse than the baseline because of false-positive tests.
numbers: HotPotQA with ground-truth context: self-reflection gave an 8% absolute boost over an episodic-memory-only variant. HumanEval Rust (50 hardest): no test generation 52% vs 60% baseline; no self-reflection step: no gain over baseline; full 68%. MBPP Python: baseline 0.80, Reflexion 0.77. False-positive test rate 16.3% on MBPP Python vs 1.4% on HumanEval Python.
limits: Small subsets (50 hardest Rust problems). Authors attribute MBPP result to weak test suites; not independently confirmed.
agent_relevance: A no-good is only as good as the check that decided the attempt failed. Bad failure labels turn memory into harm (false conflict = wrongly pruned branch).

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Re-tested self-correction with the oracle removed. Reported gains came from using the ground-truth label to decide when to stop. Without it, accuracy drops, because models flip correct answers to wrong more often than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: 75.9 standard, 74.7 after 2 self-correction rounds (5 calls); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 43.0. With oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 95.5, GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5, HotpotQA GPT-3.5 49.0, GPT-4 59.0 (rows as printed). On GSM8K GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Tested on reasoning without external feedback. Subsets of 100-200 questions for some sets. Does not cover tool or test feedback, which Reflexion relies on.
agent_relevance: Core boundary condition: conflicts must come from an external or checkable source. A self-declared failure is not a sound conflict and must not become a no-good.

source: Ji, Lu, Zhang, Olukotun (2026) Sentry: Learning to Recover from LLM Agent Failures at Test Time (arXiv 2610.02994, preprint)
finding: Failure lessons kept in the agent's context misfire when their failure is absent. Removing failure lessons from an evolving playbook improved held-out scores. Putting the full playbook into context lowered scores even when the same lessons were available on demand.
numbers: ACE playbook with failure lessons removed: WebShop reward 0.335 to 0.391; Mind2Web Replay completion 0.562 to 0.643. Fixed playbook added to persistent context: WebShop 0.364 to 0.296, Mind2Web Replay 0.651 to 0.599. Runtime intervention without a need check: WebShop 0.136 vs 0.170 unassisted. Qwen3.5-9B, five runs.
limits: Single preprint, small open model, not peer reviewed. Authors designed the comparison to favour their principle. Benchmarks are web and tool tasks, not search problems.
agent_relevance: Direct analogy to CDCL's watched literals and clause deletion: a stored constraint should be examined only when its trigger condition holds. Do not paste the whole no-good list into the prompt.

source: Ji et al. (2026) Sentry (arXiv 2610.02994)
finding: Sentry detects a failure, retrieves matching lessons from an external store, checks that the agent recovers (without task reward), and stores a new lesson only if recovery is verified. It beat runtime-intervention and context-evolution baselines.
numbers: Qwen3.5-9B, mean of five runs. WebShop reward 0.468 vs best baseline 0.264 (Wink), base 0.170. AppWorld pass 38.53% vs 27.56%, base 25.59%. SWE-bench Lite 0.30 vs 0.24, base 0.20. Mind2Web Replay 0.736 vs 0.687, base 0.420. Held-out: Sentry 0.495 vs ACE 0.335 on WebShop (+47.8%); ACE+Sentry 0.555. Resolves 81.7% of 939 detected failures. Forked replays: local recovery 33.5% to 60.5%.
limits: Gains on SWE-bench Lite are small (0.02 to 0.06 on a 0.20 base). Recovery on that benchmark only 34.0%. Verification relies on own recovery check.
agent_relevance: A measured LLM analogue of 'learn a clause only after the conflict is verified, apply it only when it fires'.

source: Ji et al. (2026) Sentry (arXiv 2610.02994)
finding: Ablations: how specific the retrieval is and whether the need for intervention is checked both matter a lot.
numbers: Retrieval by broad failure type only: -11.3% relative to full Sentry; unfiltered playbook: -18.8%; random entries: -28.9%. k=3 and k=10 retrieved entries: -4.5% and -6.2% vs k=5. Removing the intervention-need check: -54.7% average on two benchmarks. Without soft repair WebShop 0.136 (-70.9%).
limits: Relative drops averaged over two benchmarks; same preprint caveats.
agent_relevance: The worth of a no-good store is mostly in matching: a lesson triggered by the wrong failure is worse than none. Matching rule needs as much design as the lesson.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST, arXiv 2503.13657)
finding: Annotated failure study of 7 multi-agent frameworks. Step repetition is one of the most common failure modes: agents redo the same step, the thing a no-good would block.
numbers: 1642 annotated traces; failure rate of 41% to 86.7% across seven open-source systems; step repetition (FM-1.3) 15.7% of failures; not recognising task completion 12.4%; failing to follow task requirements 11.8%. Annotator agreement Cohen's kappa 0.88 in final rounds; LLM judge kappa 0.77.
limits: Prevalence counts from annotated failed runs, not controlled tests. Mostly GPT-4 era models.
agent_relevance: Gives a base rate (about 1 in 6 failures) for the repeat-attempt problem, to size the possible benefit of a repeat-blocker.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Where LLM Agents Fail and How They Can Learn From Failures (arXiv 2509.25370)
finding: AgentDebug finds the root-cause step of a failed trajectory and gives corrective feedback. Targeted feedback beat the strongest baseline. Only the abstract page was read.
numbers: +24% all-correct accuracy and +17% step accuracy vs strongest baseline on AgentErrorBench; up to 26% relative gain in task success on ALFWorld, GAIA and WebShop.
limits: Abstract only (the PDF would not parse). Gains are relative and baseline levels not read.
agent_relevance: Support for conflict analysis in the CDCL sense: locate the culprit decision, not just the final failure, before recording the lesson.

source: Search record (2026-10-26) for LLM agents that store failures as formal no-goods
finding: Two search passes (web search, standard and extended) for CDCL, no-good or clause learning applied to LLM agents found no paper that implements formal no-good learning with backjumping for an LLM agent and measures it. Closest are Reflexion, Sentry and AgentDebug (free-text or playbook lessons).
numbers: 0 direct hits in two search passes. Not a proof of absence.
limits: Search engine summaries only; no exhaustive arXiv or Semantic Scholar sweep completed.
agent_relevance: Our CDCL-style no-goods idea has no direct published measurement; SCHEMA row should be marked 'analogy, untested'.
